## AI, in plain English

**AI (artificial intelligence)** is the broad idea of making computers do tasks that normally need human-like abilities—such as understanding language, recognizing images, making predictions, or choosing an action. **Machine learning (ML)** is one way to build AI: rather than writing every rule by hand, people give a system examples/data so it can find patterns and improve its output.

IBM’s overview groups AI in two useful ways: by **capability** (how broad its abilities are) and by **function** (how it behaves). IBM notes that categories can overlap and terminology can vary.

### Three major AI capability types (IBM)
- **Narrow AI (the AI we have today):** Built for a particular kind of task. A spam filter, voice assistant, recommendation system, or chatbot can be very capable in its area, but it does not have broad human-style understanding. IBM says even ChatGPT is Narrow AI because it is limited to text-based chat.
- **General AI / AGI (theoretical):** A hypothetical AI that could carry skills from one setting to another and learn to do any intellectual task a person can do. It does not currently exist.
- **Super AI (theoretical):** A hypothetical AI that would exceed human abilities in thinking, reasoning, learning, and judgment. It also does not currently exist.

IBM also describes **reactive AI** (uses only the information in front of it) and **limited-memory AI** (uses recent/past data to help decide what to do). For example, IBM places generative-AI tools and virtual assistants in the limited-memory category.

### Three main machine-learning approaches (IBM)
- **Supervised learning:** Train with examples that already have the right answer attached—like emails marked “spam” or “not spam.” The model learns to predict the answer for new examples.
- **Unsupervised learning:** Give the system data without answer labels and ask it to find useful structure—for example, grouping customers with similar behavior.
- **Reinforcement learning:** Let a system learn through trial, feedback, and rewards—like teaching a game-playing program which moves lead to better outcomes.

IBM’s ML overview also lists semi-supervised and self-supervised learning.  
IBM sources: [Types of AI](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/artificial-intelligence-types) · [Types of machine learning](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/machine-learning-types)

## Hardware example: Intel Granite Rapids-WS vs. AMD Threadripper

Tom’s Hardware reported on **September 29, 2025** that a benchmark listing showed an upcoming Intel **Granite Rapids-WS** workstation CPU with **86 cores**, **172 threads**, and a boost clock of **up to 4.8 GHz**. The report compares it with AMD’s Threadripper **9995WX**, which has **96 Zen 5 cores**. It adds that Granite Rapids can scale to **128 cores**, although that was not confirmed as a Granite Rapids-WS product specification; separately, earlier leaks mentioned up to **128 PCIe 5.0 lanes** and **eight-channel DDR5 memory** support. In short: Intel appeared to be preparing a high-core-count workstation chip that could come much closer to AMD’s flagship Threadripper than its prior workstation CPUs—but the reported Granite Rapids-WS details were based on a listing/leaks, not a final product announcement.

Tom’s Hardware article: [Intel aims at AMD’s Threadripper with Granite Rapids-WS](https://www.tomshardware.com/pc-components/cpus/intel-aims-at-amds-threadripper-with-its-new-granite-rapids-ws-cpu-chip-armed-with-core-count-approaching-the-flagship-amd-threadripper-9995wx-boasts-a-4-8ghz-boost-clock)

### Why chips like these matter for AI and advanced computing

AI work often involves processing enormous datasets, running many calculations simultaneously, and moving data quickly between memory, storage, CPUs, and AI accelerators such as GPUs. Lots of CPU cores and threads help with parallel jobs and data preparation; large, fast memory support and plentiful PCIe lanes help keep accelerators and high-speed storage supplied with data. That is why capable workstation/server chips matter not only for AI, but also for scientific simulation, video production, engineering, and other demanding tasks. For many large AI training jobs, specialized GPU/AI accelerators do much of the model computation, while a powerful CPU platform supports and feeds the whole system.
